pages.x: In 1095 the Byzantine emperor asked the pope for soldiers against the Seljuk Turks. At Clermont in France, Pope Urban II called on Christians to march east and free Jerusalem, promising that the journey would wipe away their sins. The crowd shouted: God wills it!

Before the knights were ready, tens of thousands of poor people set off behind a preacher, Peter the Hermit. On the way, crusaders massacred the Jews of Rhineland towns such as Mainz and Worms. Most of the marchers were killed by the Turks soon after they crossed into Asia.

After three years, a sick and starving army reached Jerusalem and stormed it on 15 July 1099, massacring the Muslims and Jews inside. Godfrey of Bouillon, chosen to rule, would not wear a crown of gold where Christ had worn thorns, and took the title Defender of the Holy Sepulchre.

The crusaders set up four states along the coast, Jerusalem, Antioch, Tripoli and Edessa, defended by great castles such as Krak des Chevaliers and by new orders of warrior monks, the Templars and the Hospitallers.

Saladin, sultan of Egypt and Syria, united the Muslims against them. In 1187 he trapped the crusader army on the dry hills of Hattin in the summer heat, and then took Jerusalem. Unlike the crusaders in 1099, he let most of its people go free for a ransom.

Three kings set out to win it back. The emperor Frederick Barbarossa drowned crossing a river. Richard the Lionheart of England took Acre and beat Saladin at Arsuf, but could not take Jerusalem. In 1192 they made a truce letting Christian pilgrims visit the city. The two never met.

The Fourth Crusade never reached the Holy Land. Deep in debt to Venice, the crusaders turned on Constantinople, the greatest Christian city, and sacked it in 1204. The four bronze horses that stood on St Mark's in Venice were part of the loot.

In 1212, stories say, thousands of children in France and Germany set off to free Jerusalem without weapons, sure the sea would part for them. It did not. Historians think they were mostly poor young people, and that most went home, or never got further than the ports.
The Mamluks of Egypt took the crusader castles one by one. In 1291 they stormed Acre, the last great crusader city, and the crusader states were gone.

Two centuries of crusades left bitter memories between Christians, Muslims and Jews, and between Catholic and Orthodox Christians. They also drew Europe into the trade of the East and made Venice and Genoa rich.
pts: Called by Pope Urban II in 1095
The last crusader city fell in 1291
